paragraphs: I come back to my old argument: if woman is granted an immortal soul, she must have an understanding to develop as the work of her life. And when, to make the present state more complete — though everything shows it to be only a fraction of a mighty sum — she is lured by present gratification into forgetting her great destiny, nature is thwarted; or else she was born only to procreate and rot. Or, if we grant brutes of every kind a soul, though not a rational one, the exercise of instinct and sensibility may be the step they are to take in this life towards attaining reason in the next; so that through all eternity they will lag behind man, who, for reasons we cannot tell, was given the power to attain reason in his first mode of existence.

When I discuss the particular duties of women, as I would discuss the particular duties of a citizen or a father, it will be seen that I do not mean to suggest that they should be taken out of their families — speaking, that is, of the majority. “He that hath wife and children,” says Lord Bacon, “hath given hostages to fortune; for they are impediments to great enterprises, either of virtue or mischief. Certainly the best works, and of greatest merit for the public, have proceeded from the unmarried or childless men.” I say the same of women. But the welfare of society does not rest on extraordinary exertions; and if society were more reasonably organized, there would be even less need for great abilities or heroic virtues. Running a family and educating children particularly require understanding, in a plain, unsophisticated sense: strength of both body and mind. Yet the men who have laboured most earnestly in their writings to domesticate women have tried, with arguments dictated by a gross appetite that satiety had made fastidious, to weaken their bodies and cramp their minds. But even if, by these sinister methods, they really PERSUADED women, by working on their feelings, to stay at home and fulfil the duties of a mother and mistress of a family, I would oppose only with caution opinions that led women to right conduct by prevailing on them to make the performance of a duty the business of life, even though reason were insulted. Yet — and I appeal to experience — if, when their understanding is neglected, women are drawn away from these domestic duties as much as, or even more than, they could be by the most serious intellectual pursuit (though it may be observed that the mass of mankind will never pursue an intellectual object vigorously), I may be allowed to infer that reason is absolutely necessary for a woman to perform any duty properly; and I must repeat once more that sensibility is not reason.

The comparison with the rich still comes to my mind; for when men neglect the duties of humanity, women will do the same; a common current sweeps them both along with thoughtless speed. Wealth and honours prevent a man from enlarging his understanding and sap all his powers, by reversing the order of nature, which has always made true pleasure the reward of labour. Pleasure — enervating pleasure — is likewise within woman’s reach without her having to earn it. But until inherited property is spread more widely, how can we expect men to take pride in virtue? And until they do, women will govern them by the most direct means, neglecting their dull domestic duties to seize the pleasure that flies past on the wing of time.

“The power of women,” says some author, “is her sensibility;” and men, not seeing where this leads, do all they can to make this power swallow up every other. Those who constantly exercise their sensibility will have the most of it: poets, painters and composers, for example. Yet when sensibility is increased in this way at the expense of reason, and even of imagination, why do philosophical men complain of women’s fickleness? Man’s sexual attention acts on female sensibility in particular, and this sympathy has been exercised in women ever since their youth. A husband cannot keep up those attentions for long with the passion needed to excite lively emotions; and the heart, used to lively emotions, turns to a new lover, or pines in secret, a prey to virtue or prudence. I mean, when the heart has really been made susceptible and the taste formed; for I am inclined to conclude, from what I have seen in fashionable life, that the kind of education and the dealings between the sexes which I have condemned foster vanity more often than sensibility; and that coquetry springs more often from vanity than from the inconstancy that overstrained sensibility naturally produces.

Another argument that has weighed heavily with me must, I think, carry some force with every thoughtful and benevolent heart. Girls who have been educated in this weak way are often cruelly left by their parents without any provision, and so they depend not only on the reason but on the generosity of their brothers. These brothers, to take the most favourable view of the matter, are decent enough men, and give as a favour what children of the same parents had an equal right to. A docile woman may remain in this ambiguous, humiliating situation for some time with a tolerable degree of comfort. But when the brother marries, as he probably will, she goes from being regarded as the mistress of the family to being viewed with averted looks as an intruder, an unnecessary burden on the benevolence of the master of the house and his new partner.

Who can count up the misery that many unfortunate beings, weak alike in mind and body, suffer in such situations — unable to work and ashamed to beg? The wife, a cold-hearted, narrow-minded woman (and this is not an unfair supposition, for the present kind of education does no more to enlarge the heart than the understanding), is jealous of the little kindness her husband shows his relations; and since her sensibility does not rise as far as humanity, she is displeased to see the property of HER children squandered on a helpless sister.

These are facts that have come before my eyes again and again. The result is obvious: the wife resorts to cunning to undermine the habitual affection she is afraid to oppose openly; and neither tears nor caresses are spared until the spy is worked out of her home and thrown on the world, unprepared for its difficulties; or else sent off, as a great effort of generosity or out of some regard for propriety, with a small allowance and an uncultivated mind, into joyless solitude.

These two women may be much on a level in reason and humanity; and had they changed places, each might have played exactly the same selfish part. But had they been educated differently, the case would also have been very different. The wife would not have had that sensibility which centres on self, and reason might have taught her not to expect her husband’s affection, nor even to be flattered by it, if it led him to violate prior duties. She would wish to love him not merely because he loved her, but for his virtues; and the sister might have been able to fend for herself instead of eating the bitter bread of dependence.

I am indeed convinced that the heart, as well as the understanding, is opened by cultivation; and also — though this may seem less obvious — by strengthening the organs. I am not speaking now of momentary flashes of sensibility, but of affections. And perhaps the hardest task in educating both sexes is to adjust instruction so that it neither narrows the understanding while the heart is warmed by the generous juices of spring, just raised by the electric fermentation of the season, nor dries up the feelings by occupying the mind with inquiries remote from life.

As for women, when they are given a careful education, they are made either into fine ladies, brimming with sensibility and teeming with capricious fancies, or into mere notable women — busy, capable housewives. The latter are often friendly, honest creatures, with a shrewd kind of good sense joined to worldly prudence, which often makes them more useful members of society than the fine sentimental lady, though they have neither greatness of mind nor taste. The intellectual world is closed to them; take them out of their family or neighbourhood and they come to a standstill, for the mind finds nothing to do; literature offers a fund of amusement that they have never tried to enjoy, and have often despised. The sentiments and taste of more cultivated minds seem ridiculous to them, even in those whom chance and family ties have led them to love; and in mere acquaintances they think it all affectation.

A man of sense can love such a woman only because of her sex, and respect her because she is a trustworthy servant. To keep his own peace, he lets her scold the servants and go to church in clothes made of the very best materials. A man whose understanding was the same size as hers would probably not get on so well with her, for he might want to encroach on her prerogative and manage some household matters himself. Yet women whose minds have not been enlarged by cultivation, and whose natural selfishness of sensibility has not been widened by reflection, are very unfit to manage a family; for, stretching their power beyond its due, they are always tyrannizing to support a superiority that rests only on the arbitrary distinction of fortune. Sometimes the evil is more serious: servants are deprived of innocent pleasures and made to work beyond their strength so that the notable woman can keep a better table and outshine her neighbours in finery and display. If she attends to her children, it is generally to dress them expensively; and whether this attention springs from vanity or from doting fondness, it is equally harmful.

Besides, how many women of this kind spend their days, or at least their evenings, in discontent. Their husbands admit that they are good managers and chaste wives, but leave home to look for more agreeable — if I may use an expressive French word — piquant company; and the patient drudge who performs her task like a blind horse in a mill is cheated of her just reward; for the wages due to her are her husband’s caresses, and women with so few resources in themselves do not bear this deprivation of a natural right very patiently.

A fine lady, on the other hand, has been taught to look down with contempt on the ordinary occupations of life, though she has been encouraged only to acquire accomplishments that rise one degree above mere sense; for even bodily accomplishments cannot be acquired with any precision unless the understanding has been strengthened by exercise. Without a foundation of principles, taste is superficial, and grace must spring from something deeper than imitation. Her imagination, however, is inflamed, and her feelings made fastidious, if not corrupted by artifice; or else no counterweight of judgment is acquired while the heart still remains guileless, though it grows too tender.

These women are often amiable, and their hearts really are more responsive to general benevolence, more alive to the sentiments that civilize life, than the square-elbowed family drudge; but, lacking a due proportion of reflection and self-government, they only inspire love. They are their husbands’ mistresses for as long as they keep any hold on their affections, and the platonic friends of his male acquaintances. These are the fair defects in nature: the women who seem to have been created not to enjoy the companionship of man, but to save him from sinking into absolute brutality by rubbing off the rough corners of his character, and by playful dalliance to lend some dignity to the appetite that draws him to them. Gracious Creator of the whole human race! Have you created such a being as woman, who can trace your wisdom in your works and feel that you alone are by your nature exalted above her — for no better purpose? Can she believe that she was made only to submit to man, her equal, a being who, like her, was sent into the world to acquire virtue? Can she consent to be occupied merely with pleasing him, merely with adorning the earth, when her soul is capable of rising to you? And can she rest in supine dependence on man for reason, when she ought to climb with him the steep and arduous heights of knowledge?

Yet if love is the supreme good, let women be educated only to inspire it, and let every charm be polished to intoxicate the senses; but if they are moral beings, let them have a chance to become intelligent, and let love for man be only one part of that glowing flame of universal love which, after encircling humanity, rises in grateful incense to God.
